#5085. Ledger Confirms Tampered Bitcoin Wallets in Berlin as Spy Implant Probe Spreads Beyond Asia

Ledger Confirms Tampered Bitcoin Wallets in Berlin as Spy Implant Probe Spreads Beyond Asia

The tampered Ledger wallets aren’t just a Southeast Asia problem anymore.

Ledger said Wednesday it has confirmed tampered hardware wallets in Berlin and is investigating reports of two more in Dubai, expanding a probe it had previously described as a localized incident in Southeast Asia.

“Our findings since then show tampered devices outside Southeast Asia. It is the same incident,” the company said in an update on its support site.

The investigation began last month after customers who bought devices from reseller CryptoBilis reported losses. Onchain investigators traced a suspected drain of about $87 million from hundreds of victim wallets across Ethereum, Tron, and Bitcoin.

Ledger said at the time that all confirmed cases were tied to CryptoBilis, and it later asked resellers in seven Asian markets to pull devices from sale.

Every device Ledger has confirmed shows the same kind of physical modification, designed to capture a user’s recovery phrase during setup. A recovery phrase, typically a string of 24 words, is the master key to a crypto wallet: anyone who has it can drain the funds.

Our investigation into the hardware implant incident we disclosed Oct 15th is ongoing, and we published an update: https://t.co/wx6mfQPr99

There is no flaw in Ledger's secure chip or operating system, and no confirmed case involving a device bought on https://t.co/vQ4QWa1D0f

Ledger maintains there’s no flaw in its secure chip or operating system and no confirmed case involving a device bought on ledger.com.

In Germany, Ledger said a few tampered units were localized to Berlin, and it urged anyone who bought a Ledger device there since January 2026 to contact support.

In Dubai, it’s working with distribution partners to learn how two suspected units entered circulation. Those devices were bought at a Virgin Megastore location, according to multiple reports. Ledger also found one affected Nano Gen5 among the Southeast Asian resellers it previously paused.

The company expects more tampered devices to surface, though it says the number remains small overall. Its Donjon security team is examining suspected devices, and Ledger has asked resellers to pause sales wherever inspections are ongoing.

Customers worried about a device should stop using it, Ledger said. It advises moving funds to a new wallet created on a device bought directly from ledger.com, without reusing the old recovery phrase or passphrase, since a tampered device can capture both. It also recommends filing a report with local authorities.

For a limited time, Ledger is offering physical inspections, including X-rays, at its factory in Vierzon, France.

“We will never ask for your recovery phrase,” the company said on X.

The last few months have been a rough stretch for hardware wallet markers overall. Rival manufacturer Trezor said this week that hackers who breached a third-party shipping partner likely took information tied to about 27,000 orders. That’s the company’s third such breach in as many months.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

THE MOST CONVENIENT travel companion is a backpack, and I envy those who can pack a trip’s worth of clothing into one. But I need a carry-on suitcase; I like to think of it as option packing instead of overpacking. For years I relied on my Filson Duffle—and still love it as a weekender—but found myself wanting a roller bag for hands-free travel and to get a little more organization.

Carry-on suitcases are quite bland though. They’re plastic boxes that require you to attach a keychain or bandana just to recognize your own. I considered Rimowa’s iconic carry-ons for a short while until I remembered my tax bracket and came back to reality (if you’re unfamiliar, they’re expensive). More palatable aluminum options from Away and Monos exist, but they miss the mark for me, be it style or features.

A lucky typo while searching Porter Yoshida bags led me to Portar luggage. The brand’s aluminum and polycarbonate/aluminum luggage is sleek, durable, and costs a fifth of a Rimowa cabin bag. I used the Portar Aluminum Carry-On Luggage all summer and it exceeded my expectations, and it’s now seeing me through holiday travel.

Portar’s carry-on is exactly what I was looking for lookswise—an unbranded aluminum suitcase with leather handles. Functionally, it surpassed expectations after trips to Michigan, Chicago, Houston, and Amsterdam.

The aluminum shell has held up to TSA's less-than-careful hands over the past couple of months. Aluminum luggage gathers minor dings and scuffs throughout travel—it’s part of the charm—but the black covers any marks I may have picked up, and I don’t notice any. I also like the rivets along the shell's border. It reminds me of old travel trunks I’ve seen in vintage stores.

The leather handles are not only a nice aesthetic touch, but they actually make handling the suitcase much easier. They’re substantial and padded, unlike the flimsy plastic strip you see on a lot of carry-on luggage. It makes hoisting it into the overhead cabin a bit more steady and secure.

The latches are also a huge change for me, as I’m used to hassling with zippers that snag or tear—I will never go back to zippered luggage again. Both the telescopic handle and wheels operate smoothly, so I glide gracefully to my gate.

Technically my fiancée’s Away carry-on has more space based on dimensions, but I swear I can efficiently pack more into my Portar. Maybe it’s the clever pocket configuration or the removable compression straps and divider, but coming back from Amsterdam, we were counting on my Portar to bring back Delft ceramics and other acquisitions. All of which fit despite my over (option!) packing.

My Portar will now accompany me home for the holidays. It will also travel to the Pitztal Valley in Austria, then on to Vienna the week after Thanksgiving. It’s a first-class carry-on in the cabin space above my economy seat. Air travel used to be luxurious, and people would dress up for the occasion of reaching 38,000 feet. The Portar carry-on is bringing back some of that charm and costs me less than $300.

#5083. The 7 Best Electric Razors for Women in 2026, Tested by Beauty Editors

It's time to ditch the disposable before your holiday party.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

My interest in hair removal started in elementary school when I snuck into my mom's medicine cabinet and dragged her razor across my leg like I was coloring with my favorite box of markers. Needless to say, I've learned the right way to shave since then (namely to apply shaving cream and gently glide my razor toward the grain with light pressure).

I've had a lot of help perfecting my technique—as a beauty editor with a decade of testing experience, I have access to the best dermatologists and aestheticians. Yet, no matter how on-point my new shaving technique is now, most women's razors never get my legs quite as smooth. And other hair removal methods are super painful, ripping strands out at the root. Ouch!

But then, I upgraded to electric razors—and I've never turned back.

“A closer shave can feel nice, but because the surface of our skin is not perfectly smooth, it inevitably results in removal of some skin cells,” says dermatologist Caroline Robinson, MD. This can lead to microscopic nicks and irritation. “Electric razors can help avoid this. They’re typically less sensitizing,” says Dr. Robinson, because the shave they provide is not as close. At-home laser hair removal devices, waxing, sugaring, and threading are all great options for hair removal if you’ve got the time (and the coin), but if silky-smooth skin sans irritation is what you’re after, the answer is electric.

Over the past two years, Women's Health editors have been testing popular electric razors to determine which seven are worth the investment. Ultimately, we found that the Philips Beauty Series was the best multi-use product due to its five-blade razor and dual-sidedness that allows for a super close shave. Meanwhile, the Remington Smooth & Silky On-the-Go Shaver delivers on quality for quick touch-ups while being budget- and travel-friendly. Read on to see our other winners from our testing process.

A favorite of our editors, this hair removal device hits all of the targets we're looking for when buying an electric razor. For starters, it literally has 40 micro-grip tweezers in its motor to provide a super close shave, keeping your skin smooth for weeks at a time. While that might seem intimidating, it upgrades your in-shower shaving routine in a major way.

You can hit even the trickiest spots on your body. From your underarms and belly down to your ankles, this electric razor has you covered quite literally from head to toe. And with an impressive 50-minute runtime you can eliminate all of my unwanted hair with this device at least a couple of times before recharging it for just an hour. You’ll also appreciate that it's lightweight but not flimsy like it'll slip out of your grip. Plus, it's waterproof so you can shave in the shower without worrying about your new razor cranking out mid-shave.

An upgrade from the original Braun model, the more expensive but higher-tech Flex comes with a flexible head (hence, the name) that can uniquely adapt to your body's curves and contours—even the complicated corners of your bikini line. In addition to the epilator, the bundle also comes with a body exfoliation brush, skin contact cap for additional comfort, and more—definitely a bargain.

"The face and body brushes are especially useful, and I love how you can interchange the heads depending on what type of cleansing you want to do," says Women's Health contributor Isabel McMahon.

She credits the device’s built-in light, called the "smartlight," as a great option for women who like dimmer lighting while showering but still want to see what they're doing.

We previously tried and enjoyed the Philips Lady Shaver Series 6000, but it's no longer available. Thankfully, the brand upgraded to the 9000 model—and we love the changes.

You're paying $30 more, but it's worth the upgrade. The new model is a more powerful device that has two speed settings for faster plucking. It also features a quicker two-hour recharge time and can be used cordless for up to an hour.

The 9000 is equipped with eight attachments, including a floating foil head that glides across the skin. The different blades of the Philips electric razor are designed to target specific areas of your body, like the more compact bikini trimmer comb and head versus the larger trimming comb for your legs. It does an excellent job of trimming coarse body hair without any irritation or tugging.

Regardless of which attachment you employ, they all ensure that you can shave safely, even in the tightest contours of your legs and underarms. Whether you shave wet or dry, the ergonomic handle design will make sure nothing slips through your fingers. For this reason, we think the Philips is an incredible value. There are other, less expensive options on our list, but they're not quite as versatile in terms of where you can use them, so that's why this one took the top value spot.

Looking to stay silky-smooth on vacay? Then click “add to cart” on this extremely travel-friendly razor and then toss it in your carry-on or gym bag for quick, simple touch-ups. It's compact, so it won't take up precious room in your cosmetic bag (you could even stash it in your office drawer to ensure that you're hair-free for any impromptu after-work activities like happy hours and date nights). And yep, this little shaver is super lightweight to carry which is always a win.

Despite being battery-powered, you'll be shocked by how durable it is compared to something cheaper. This dual trimmer lifts and guides the blades for smooth results whether you're shaving wet or dry. It does a great job for the price, but you might notice that it seems to work best when the hair is longer, so it may not be ideal for targeting stubble. (It's totally NBD, though, because you can just shave less often and ultimately who doesn't love that?)

It's also not waterproof or durable for daily, consistent use so you wouldn't want to consider this your primary hair remover, but for a quick trip—brilliant! No wonder it earned an impressive 4.1-star average from more than 14,430 Amazon reviews.

Our favorite Philips model is no longer being sold, but we found a much cheaper alternative that doesn’t skimp on quality. After all, it can be nerve-racking to take an epilator or electric razor to the face, but this compact model was made just for that.

It’s shaped like a lipstick tube and features a hypoallergenic head that glides over rogue chin hairs and your upper lip with ease. Though it lacks a built-in mirror or LED light so you can conveniently see and remove even the smallest facial hairs, this device is only $20 compared to the $47 Philips model. With those savings you could easily treat yourself to a light up makeup to ensure you see every unwanted hair.

"I love this face shaver when I'm having one of those all-out spa nights," says Wohlner. She notes that, when paired with a liquid exfoliant and a hydrating face mask, the results are truly out of this world.

Pro tip: You should try using it before your skincare routine to help your products to really penetrate the skin for a major glow. Just don't use anything with too many active ingredients like retinol right after as that can cause sensitivity.

Amazon reviewers can’t get enough of this affordable electric razor. It boasts a casual 4.2-star average from nearly 15,500 Amazon reviews. No wonder it earned the top spot as Amazon’s number one bestselling electric razor. So what makes it so effective for you? It does a little bit of everything well! There are five interchangeable heads that target everything from the bikini area and legs to underarms and face. If you’re dealing with rogue hairs in hard-to-reach areas, use this one for touchups. It comes with trimmers and traditional razor heads so you can snip longer hairs to about the length of a rice grain before shaving. Offering IPX7 waterproof protection, you can confidently shave in the shower with this device or use it dry if you prefer.

This Philips electric razor has a large head and self-sharpening blade to rapidly remove facial hair. Wohlner considers this tool as the most effective method for eliminating stubborn upper lip and chin hairs. "While it's too big to remove hair on my brows, it's awesome for those larger areas of the face when you're short on time and want to look smooth and stubble-free," she says.

This shaver has a hypoallergenic stainless steel head that doesn’t irritate sensitive skin, quickly removing unwanted hair in a single pass without causing pain or discomfort. The Series 5000 keeps Wohlner's face smooth, and it always glides over the skin effortlessly without leaving it red and raw. It even comes with a built-in mirror in the cap to touch-up on the go.

Pro tip: The large shaver head does tend to get clogged after a few uses, which can be prevented if you wipe it down with alcohol after every use. Taking care of your device will ensure you get the closest shave and that it lasts for years.

This razor, which is specifically designed for the bikini and underarm areas, can be used both inside and outside the shower, no matter your hair type. It's ideal for thick, coarser hair, though, because it has a sharp blade that trims them on the first attempt. Additionally, this cordless device has rounded edges to prevent accidents. Anyone who's shaved knows hair removal can get messy, but the head on this shaver opens up for easy rinsing, too.

You’ll appreciate how beginner-friendly the Philips razor is. The instructions are so clear and easy to follow, which make your experience a breeze. The electric razor is relatively small and very easy to get a secure grip on, so anyone with butterfingers can rely on this device.I tried this razor and think it's pretty sweet, especially when cleaning up my bikini line. At first I was nervous that my longer hairs would get caught in the razor (it was winter, please let me live), but I was pleasantly surprised that it was a nonissue. It actually gets down quite low, especially when I don't use the comb attachment.

I enjoyed my bikini line shaving experience enough to use this device on my underarms and that's when I realized it heats up relatively quickly, which may be something to keep in mind if you're going for a longer shave sesh. Unlike the sold out Gillette razor we featured, Philips is rechargeable, so you won’t have to buy batteries once it dies out.

With the multitude of options available on Amazon, Ulta, and Dermstore, there are a couple of features to consider the next time you're in the market for a fresh shave:

More is not always better. In fact, a larger number of blades can sometimes increase irritation, says dermatologist Lauren Ploch, MD. On the other hand, fewer blades mean more passes over the skin, which can also cause irritation. It's about finding a happy medium that works for you. This may take some testing, so remember to try out your razor on a small patch of skin to see how you react before going all in.

Think about how well a razor feels and fits in your hand. You want something that’s well-balanced and not too heavy for the most comfortable shaving experience. Also consider if it will shave wet or dry. Not all electric razors can be used in the shower, Dr. Ploch points out. So, if you're a shower shaver, make sure to grab something waterproof and cordless.

You also want to make sure your razor head can contour to your body's curves, especially when you're targeting areas like the bikini line, underarms, toes, and even legs. Some of the razors on this list, like the Panasonic Close Curves Electric Razor, can uniquely adapt to the body's curves with their rotating heads.

If a razor is rechargeable (big plus already), make sure to check how long it takes to charge and the battery life. If you don't want to deal with a cord or annoying charge time, some of the options on this list—hi, Philips Series 5000 Electric Facial Hair Remover—are battery-powered, which may be more convenient while traveling.

Some razors come with trimmers, blade guides, and changeable blade heads for different areas of the body. If you're looking for more of a Swiss Army knife-type, multi-tool situation, take a look at the available attachments. Then, see if those are compatible with the parts of your body you want to tackle.

Believe it or not, many razors have a warranty, so if you're unsatisfied with your purchase, you can most likely return it for a longer period than you might think. Most razors on this list have a 30-day warranty, which gives you ample time for testing.

Our team tests a wide range of products and services to provide our readers with reliable, honest, and trustworthy information. It's our belief that our readers deserve the best, which is why our recommendations have been thoroughly tested and vetted by our very own editors. For the past year, Women’s Health editors, including myself, and contributors Jasmine Gomez and Sabrina Talbert, tested the bestselling, most popular, and top-rated electric razors. Our team also consulted four dermatologists, and then evaluated thousands of customer reviews and ratings to narrow down the seven best electric razors for a wide range of needs and preferences.

Ready for smooth, bump-free skin? Look no further than these editor-tested and expert-approved electric razors for women, below.

If you struggle with bumps and irritation, an electric razor might be your new best friend. Of course, you still need to make sure you use that electric razor properly. Dermatologists say you should follow the below best practices for a smooth shave every time.

Make sure your skin is well hydrated before shaving because using an electric razor over dry, irritated skin can make matters worse, says dermatologist Joshua Zeichner, MD. Dr. Robinson adds that you should also use a gentle cleanser prior to shaving. And, avoid fragrance or products known to cause irritation immediately before and after shaving, she says.

And please, do so in the direction of the hair growth, says Dr. Zeichner. Repeated strokes over the same area increase the likelihood of irritation and ingrown hairs.

Hydration is key. "I advise patients that they do not need a dedicated post-shave or aftercare lotion—a gentle moisturizer is just fine in these areas," says Dr. Robinson, who likes light, fragrance-free formulas. Aside from that, Dr. Robinson recommends making sure you follow any specific instructions on the product package—in other words, you should actually read the directions.

At the end of the day, everyone's going to have their personal preference, and it's not worth, ahem, splitting hairs if you prefer one type of razor over another. That being said, if your skin is prone to irritation, it might be time to ditch the traditional razor. With an electric razor, you’re not scraping against the skin really hard like a traditional razor does, says dermatologist Cameron Rokhsar, MD. This means that you won't see a lot of the cuts and burns that sometimes result from a manual blade, says Dr. Rokhsar. There are also areas of the body that might be better suited to shave with an electric razor. "Most women's electric razors are designed for our curvy areas," says Dr. Ploch. "I prefer electric razors around the ankles because manual razors cut this area easily."

Keeping your electric razor clean is incredibly important, says Dr. Rokhsar. Many derms will recommend changing a manual razor every time you shave, but you can't do that with an electric one, which makes running the blades under warm water after use a crucial step. This will keep it free of hair, shaving cream, and other residues.

Dr. Rokhsar also recommends swiping over the blades and the outside of the razor with a rubbing alcohol-soaked cotton ball regularly. "Especially if it sits in your bathroom moisture, bacteria will accumulate on the blades," he says. "It's an easy entry point for bacteria to go down the hair follicle." That's a big no-no if you want to stay free of irritation or infection.

Our team of editors follow Dr. Rokhsar's advice and it hasn't led us astray. And despite evaluating some of these razors for close to a year, we are pleased that we haven't noticed any rusting after using the alcohol-soaked cotton ball.

Another tip is to actually read and follow the maintenance instructions of your device. (Admittedly, we threw ours away since we've been using these for several months and like to keep the limited space of our beauty closet as streamlined as possible.) You can also prioritize using devices like the Philips Series 5000 Electric Facial Hair Remover that's easy to clean, as the head can easily be removed so you can dump shaved hair and dead skin cells straight into the garbage.

#5082. DCG’s Zcash miner Fortitude clears vote for Nasdaq listing as ZEC retreats from all-time high

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The Zcash miner plans to trade as TUDE after closing its HeartSciences merger, with Nasdaq listing approval still pending.

Zcash miner Fortitude has cleared another hurdle to going public after HeartSciences shareholders approved a merger between the two.

Roughly 86% of votes from Thursday's meeting supported the deal, Fortitude said in a Friday release. Fortitude now needs to get Nasdaq listing approval. Once completed, the combined company will take on the name Fortitude Mining Group and expects to trade under the ticker TUDE. A listing date has not been set.

"Today’s vote paves the way for Fortitude to become a premier publicly traded Zcash mining platform," CEO Jaime Leverton said in a statement.

Fortitude, which spun out of Digital Currency Group's Foundry mining operations in January 2025, currently has 60 MW of power capacity across its seven U.S. sites.

Its operating Zcash hashrate metric has grown nearly 15% to 5.4 GSol/s from 4.7 GSol/s reported in early October.

Last month, Fortitude signed a letter of intent with mining hardware manufacturer Bitmain to be first in line for its next-gen Zcash miners. This included a non-binding commitment to purchase up to $100 million in equipment. That followed a July agreement to buy 9,000 of Bitmain's Z15 Pro machines for a total of $31.5 million.

Fortitude sells or monetizes all the ZEC it mines, according to Friday's release. It also expects to contribute $2 million in ZEC at the merger's closing to help fund transaction costs and other expenses.

ZEC traded around $753 on Friday, down roughly 55% from its all-time high of $1,680 reached about two months ago. Despite the pullback, it remains among the strongest performers year to date among the top 20 cryptocurrencies, alongside Hyperliquid's HYPE.

#5081. Bitcoin Price Slips to Lows Not Seen Since 2024, Nasdaq Plunges 5%

The bitcoin price slid to near $58,300 on Friday afternoon, down about 6.2% over the past 24 hours, according to Look Into Bitcoin data, as a deepening selloff in chip and artificial intelligence stocks sent the Nasdaq down about 5% and pushed bitcoin just under its summer low.

Bitcoin broke below $60,000 late Friday morning, a few hours after this morning’s report had it near $61,500. Over the past 24 hours, the bitcoin price has traded between $57,655 and $62,562, a drop of about $3,880. Bitcoin is down about 25% in November, on pace for its worst month since June 2022.

Selling on Wall Street sped up through the afternoon. The Nasdaq Composite fell about 5% in late trading and the S&P 500 dropped about 3.5%. Yahoo Finance said the Nasdaq was on pace to close negative for the year, while the S&P 500 was poised to close in correction territory.

Chipmakers led the drop. Nvidia (NVDA) fell about 12.5% to near $128, and AMD, Broadcom and Micron also posted double-digit losses. Gold futures dropped nearly 5%. Treasury yields fell as traders rotated into bonds and defensive sectors such as consumer staples and healthcare, Reuters reported.

Anthropic (ANT) fell nearly 12% to around $86 on its first full day of trading, leaving it just above its $83 IPO price. The stock had closed its Thursday debut at $97.17 after raising $81.3 billion in the largest IPO of all time, CNBC reported.

Leveraged traders were forced out as the bitcoin price broke support. About $1.53 billion in crypto bets were wiped out over 24 hours, with long positions making up $1.4 billion of that total. Bitcoin alone accounted for around $540 million, while ether fell more than 8% to around $1,600.

Bitcoin funds have been sellers, too. Investors have pulled roughly $3.5 billion from U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs so far this month, including $582 million on Thursday. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) accounted for $541.1 million of Thursday’s withdrawals, its largest one-day outflow on record.

Rate worries are adding pressure. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pushed back Friday on calls for a half-point Federal Reserve hike in December. Traders still saw a more than 98% chance of a quarter-point increase, and some strategists warned that further hikes could deepen the selloff.

CoinShares head of research James Butterfill said the drop looks driven more by the AI stock selloff than by problems inside crypto. Bitcoin has increasingly traded alongside other growth assets that depend on easy money, he said.

The dip to $57,655 briefly took bitcoin just under its summer low near $57,700. It is also on track for a seventh straight weekly loss, its longest losing streak since 2022.

Strategy (MSTR) fell about 8.4% to near $78.90, adding to the losses after the stock fell for a sixth straight day on Thursday. Coinbase (COIN) dropped about 5.5% to near $103. Robinhood (HOOD) lost about 9.6% and Circle (CRCL) fell about 7.9%.

Bitcoin miners fared worst. MARA Holdings (MARA) sank about 17% to near $5.17, IREN (IREN) fell about 17% and CleanSpark (CLSK) dropped about 16%. Riot Platforms (RIOT) lost about 8.4%, and Galaxy Digital (GLXY) fell about 9.4%. Many miners have expanded into AI data centers, tying their shares to the chip selloff.

The bitcoin price is now down more than 50% from its record above $126,000, set in October 2025.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $58,300.

#5080. Bitcoin Struggles to Hold $64,000 as ETF Outflows Hit $2.9B in November

Bitcoin Struggles to Hold $64,000 as ETF Outflows Hit $2.9B in November

Bitcoin is struggling to hold the $64,000 level as investors continue to pull money from spot Bitcoin ETFs and brace for another interest rate hike from the Federal Reserve.

The leading cryptocurrency was trading at around $63,800 on Thursday, down 1% on the day and 13% over the past week, according to Decrypt data. It has hovered between roughly $63,000 and $65,000 since the weekend, briefly dipping below $63,000 and touching a 24-hour low of $62,068, per CoinGecko data.

"Bitcoin remains under selling pressure," Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com, told Decrypt, noting that it has fallen roughly 26% from its late-September peak near $87,000. "Elevated Treasury yields, dollar strength and expectations of further Fed tightening are weighing on risk appetite, while the broader technology selloff has added to the pressure."

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $306.4 million in net outflows on Wednesday, after $239.9 million on Tuesday, according to SoSoValue data. The funds have seen outflows on nine of the past 10 trading days, with Monday's small $8 million inflow the only exception, and have lost about $2.9 billion so far in November. Their total net assets have fallen to $77.7 billion. Bitcoin miners have added to the selling, with major miners including Riot and MARA selling some of their holdings to fund a shift into AI infrastructure.

Monday's brief inflow "does not signal a market inflection point," Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey, told Decrypt. Net short positions in Bitcoin futures held by leveraged funds on CME have fallen to their lowest level since early 2023, and futures basis yields have narrowed, he said, indicating that hedge funds have largely unwound the basis trade that paired spot ETF purchases with short futures. That means the current outflows are mainly driven by investors actively cutting their Bitcoin exposure, Sun said.

"If macro expectations do not improve, investors may shift from buying the dip to selling into rallies, creating additional overhead resistance on subsequent rebounds," he added.

"Recent Bitcoin ETF outflows and leveraged liquidations" have amplified the decline, Hathorn said. "Despite stronger Nvidia earnings, the market has struggled to stage a significant rebound, suggesting confidence remains fragile. A sustained recovery may require renewed ETF inflows and a more supportive interest-rate outlook."

Some traders have also pointed the finger at Anthropic's upcoming IPO for drawing money away from crypto, though analysts have disputed that the listing is draining crypto liquidity, attributing it instead to ETF outflows, forced selling and rising interest rates.

Traders see a 90.7% chance that the Fed will raise rates by a quarter point at its December 9 meeting, and a 9.3% chance of a half-point hike, according to CME FedWatch. The odds of a half-point move have risen from 6.5% a day earlier. Fed Governor Christopher Waller has called for an even bigger, half-point increase, unless policymakers signal another rise in January.

Hathorn said $64,000 is the immediate level to watch, followed by support around $62,000 and the psychological $60,000 mark. A sustained recovery above $66,000 to $68,000 could ease selling pressure, "but the broader trend remains bearish while lower highs persist," she said.

Onchain analytics firm Glassnode said in its weekly report on Tuesday that the crash had pushed investors’ realized losses to levels seen only near past market lows in 2018, 2020, 2022 and early 2023, a sign of capitulation. Bitcoin is now holding a dense block of recent buyers between $62,000 and $66,000, which grew by about 66,000 BTC during the two days of heaviest selling, Glassnode said. But a daily close below that block could set off a fast drop toward the June low of $58,500, and the Realized Price, the average price at which all Bitcoin last moved, at $53,700.

Traders on Decrypt Predict see a 43% chance that Bitcoin will fall to $60,000 at some point before the end of November, and a 12% chance that it will drop as low as $55,000. They give just a 2% chance that it will climb back to $82,500 this month.

There are some signs of support. About 1.1 million BTC, roughly 5.5% of supply, last changed hands at prices between $60,000 and $64,000, and that band has grown by more than 25,000 BTC in recent days, according to Neil Steinhardt, head of Nexo U.S., in a note shared with Decrypt Wednesday. A dense base of holders with costs near current prices "can act as a support zone, though it is not a floor," he wrote.

Bitcoin has also held up better than gold. The amount of gold one Bitcoin buys rose above its 200-day average this week, to about 17.1 ounces, around 40% above its March low, Steinhardt said.

#5079. There’s No Irony in The Armored League. Only Steel.

Welcome to NYC’s extremely violent, surprisingly wholesome new combat scene.

“THERE’S A LOT more work to do,” Damion DiGrazia muses, as 30 or so individuals spread themselves out across the gymnasium at the Manhattanville Community Center in Harlem. A pair of double doors swings lazily back and forth, marking a procession of students and the boxes they carry. DiGrazia leans against the wall, dressed in a red polo and khaki trousers, watching his small community unpack and ready itself for training.

The class does not have a format in the traditional sense. There is no lantern-jawed instructor with a whistle and a clipboard. No snap of uniforms in sync with the rhythm of a kata. There is not even, as far as I could tell, a formal warm-up. Instead, the room seems to have its own sense of internal order.

A group forms around the pieces of armor to begin the painstaking process of polishing and assessing each one for damage or repairs. Some—a breastplate, maybe a set of greaves—are singled out and ferried to a corner, where three individuals sit, cross-legged, and carefully hammer out the dents.

Ropes are thrown over the basketball hoops, and as soon as they land, students appear and begin practicing striking drills with blunted steel weapons. There are, admittedly, a lot of people with weapons. It’s a little surreal at first. When you encounter a fighter in full armor with a sword and buckler or a mace, there is a sense of visual cohesion. It is an entirely different matter to pass a fighter in cutoff denim and a T-shirt practicing elegant, sweeping strikes with an axe.

At the back of the room, the mats find their way into a rectangle, and small scrimmages begin with foam swords and shields. The training takes on its own rhythm; newer members train with foam swords and shields around the edges of the room, while the more seasoned fighters, now sporting what appear to be hockey helmets with face masks, begin grappling practice at its center. Everyone seems to know where they need to be and what they need to do.

It’s taken a long time to get here—years, actually, 13 of them, to be precise. After serving in the military, DiGrazia traces a path through Columbia University, then Harvard, before landing a job at Morgan Stanley. Finding the rhythm of corporate life increasingly dull, he sought relief through extreme sports. DiGrazia started with the classics: marathons, ultramarathons, scuba diving, skydiving, martial arts. But nothing really stuck; he was always chasing something else. That is, until a happy accident. DiGrazia tried what he thought was going to be “full-contact” LARPing (live-action role-playing), but found the experience less than fulfilling: “You couldn't punch people, couldn't grapple people, couldn't kick people, nothing,” DiGrazia says. The participants were wearing plastic armor, and a hit to the leg saw fighters taking a theatrical knee and swiping at their opponents. At the end of the practice, however, DiGrazia found himself sticking around, commiserating with another fighter, Zorikh, whom he credits as starting his journey along a path that would lead to him founding Gladiators NYC, and laying the groundwork for The Armored League.

Modern armored combat has a longer history in Europe, and DiGrazia found himself bouncing all over the continent, fighting in Poland or next to a castle in Spain. If you wanted to fight in armor, Eastern Europe was where you had to go. Stateside, the early days were decidedly underground and homebrew. Your options were more limited: small groups of fighters met in parking lots and cornfields. Orlando Mendez, one of the founding members of Gladiators NYC, remembers “a lot of horse arenas.” They were one of the few places you could throw someone into a wall without complaint. It was a sport that grew anywhere it could find space. Jason Puerta, owner of Golden Ring Combat, a West Coast armored combat group, recalls regularly fighting on the lawns of a corporate campus after securing the bemused blessing of the local security outfit. It wasn’t quite Fight Club—new members were always welcome (and still are), and people were encouraged to talk about it. Instead, the group could be said to be self-selective: “You either got the hang of it, or you just turned in your armor at the end of the day,” DiGrazia recalls. There were few rules, no weight divisions, and no weapon classes.

In these early years, the attrition rate was high. DiGrazia estimates about half of the participants quit within weeks. Even when he first secured the community center and started spreading the word about classes, he remembers sitting on a bench in the gym, staring at the doors, waiting for someone, anyone, to come to a class. Eventually, they did.

The free classes, access to equipment, loaner armor, and the open exhibition matches in New York’s Central Park—all of these, he believes, must remain core elements of the community and the sport. Gladiators NYC also has a nonprofit arm called “Santa’s Knights” where armored knights go door to door during the holidays and deliver presents to children. His commitment to this approach has not come without difficulties. DiGrazia once partnered with a martial arts school whose owner forbade him from sponsoring students who could not afford the $30 class fee. That school closed during COVID.

Technically, the sport can trace its roots back to the 14th century, when knights, foot soldiers, and men-at-arms would practice combat using dull steel weapons and a mixture of soft and plate armor. It was a way to hone their skills in times of peace. The fundamentals of the practice remain in a number of combat sports to this day, but one need only watch a bout of Olympic fencing (or “pointy tag” as Mendez described it) to realize the distance traveled. The Armored League, however, doesn’t seek a return to its medieval origins or even to the stringently historically accurate expressions, which tend to dominate in Europe. When pressed about this, DiGrazia gives an exasperated sigh: “I don't want some librarian walking around looking with a fucking magnifying glass on everybody's goddamn rivet. Leave us alone. Let's have a good time.” The aim is to bring the spectacle and joy to new audiences.

Even if, at first, you cannot follow the scoring, the fights are pure melodrama. Like any combat sport, the fighters’ stats are announced as they enter the ring—with one key distinction: their weight includes their suit of armor. Short of a quirk, it communicates the impact of the sport in a more visceral way: when a pair of combatants crash to the ground or bounce off the chain-link fencing, that’s close to 600 pounds of flesh and steel set in ballistic motion.

Bouts are divided into three to five one-minute rounds. Points are awarded based on strikes—where they land and how hard. Basic, clean strikes with weapons, shields, or fists get a base number of points. Meanwhile headshots, two-handed weapon strikes, and slugging a downed opponent get you even more. The bouts are judged by a panel set to one side of the ring, while a pair of counters runs frantically around the perimeter counting strikes.

There are comparatively few rules beyond some basic safety precautions: no stabbing or thrusting; no stomping; no strikes at the inner elbows, armpits, or the backs of knees; no slashing at the neck; and no submissions. Save for these, anything goes, and this adds to the thrill of the fights. Fighters are also not limited to their weapons, and in some cases, they will stand and trade blows like boxers. Though all of the serious fighters have broad and varied martial arts backgrounds—and training approaches—there's a roughly consistent path that leads to The Armored League. Snatches of Muay Thai knee strikes, judo sweeps, classical boxing, escrima, and BJJ are all visible in the blur of limbs, steel, and weapons. One can only imagine how the “librarians” would feel about that.

Strikes may come in flurries or great arcs, but most are hard enough to send sparks flying off the helmets. There is a marshal in the ring with the fighters, notably unarmored save for a yellow flag that’s mainly used to break the fighters up at the end of each round, which frequently ends in a tangle of armor and weapons on the floor of the ring.

There are two elements that, despite the passage of centuries, have not changed: cost and danger. Historians are divided on the exact conversion rate between 1400 and today, and most put it in terms of wages. They quote the cost of a full set of armor at somewhere between 12 and 18 months of pay. What’s universally agreed upon is that arms and armor were (and remain) anything but cheap. A full suit—then, as now—weighs anywhere from 60 to 80 pounds.

This century, prices start at around $5,000 and climb precipitously with customization. It can take anywhere from a few weeks to a year for delivery. Most participants build their suits over time as they are drawn deeper into the sport.

Building a full set is not easy. A cursory search online will lead you to a number of pages, which might appear to offer armor, but these sites are largely focused on cosplayers or LARPers. That armor will certainly hold together for a walk through Comic-Con, but it will do little to protect from a real blow. The handful of armorers still working today have long wait lists. Puerta notes that despite this, the communal nature of the sport means that much of the armor is passed down or traded between the combatants: as someone upgrades or hangs up their helmet, the armor finds its way into a new pair of hands or onto a new person’s shoulders. At Gladiators NYC, fighters who graduate from the classes, from “softs” (padded armor), and wish to try their hand at the real thing, can borrow pieces from Gladiators NYC’s own armory.

Amongst the current fighters who regularly participate in Armored League matches, almost all fight in custom armor. The suits must adhere to certain safety standards—thickness of steel, comprehensive eye protection, etc. But beyond that, there’s ample room for self-expression.

For example, Abeid “Mando” Mitchell fights in comparatively minimalist and lightweight armor and is readily recognizable by his distinctive helmet, which was made in the style of the Mandalorian from Star Wars. Luke “The Red Knight of Brooklyn” has assembled what he refers to as “a sporting replica” of 1480s armor in keeping with his own, more classical concerns.

Despite the care and attention each fighter devotes to their own armor, at all of the matches I attended, I saw weapons traded freely, shields swapped, even gauntlets lent. For as much violence as there is inside of a 60-second round, there is an equal, if not greater, level of care at the bell. The armor is not just for show; it’s for safety. Combatants want to win as much as they want to ensure their opponent walks off the field under their own power. It’s a fine balance, and as Mendez put it, “once you put on the armor and you get your ass beat a couple of times,” everybody is basically friends.

Nevertheless, it takes a toll. Puerta told me a story of how he almost lost his left eye when the tip of a sword slipped through the bars of his helmet. Others relayed stories of being crushed in a melee and of “helmet terrors” where breathing heavily in the confines of a helmet causes a buildup of carbon dioxide and creates a sensation similar to drowning.

What does the future look like? In my time with the League and Gladiators NYC, I sensed I was watching a sport in its adolescence. It is a league and community that seems to blink in the stark light of its own success and rapidly growing audience. Social media has made it easier for these once disparate communities to connect; the cornfields and horse rinks have been parlayed into an Octagon at the Melrose Ballroom in Queens or a showcase at a theater in Times Square. The bleachers that once held a smattering of friends and family have shifted into crowds drawn from all walks of life—at the sold-out show in Queens, the lines stretched around the block and some people waited an hour just to get into the venue. The Central Park exhibition matches, which happen every second Saturday of the month, have begun to draw crowds that can number over a thousand.

DiGrazia and his merry band have come a long way from the leaner years, when they struggled to find space to practice, the years when they fought in the parking lots of regional hotels in the Midwest or in the summer heat on the boardwalk in Coney Island.

Still, there is, for now, little to no money in this sport. The community, and the fighters too, all have day jobs. They are PhD students, fitness instructors, photographers, and graphic designers. One manages a magic and costume shop. Again, Fight Club springs to mind, as each goes about their day job, bearing the marks of a Thursday brawl or a weekend match, one can only wonder if anyone sees a bruise sticking out of a shirt sleeve and stops to ask just where it came from.

We had very few cons about these leggings, but we did agree that the butt seam felt a bit too low, so they're not the most flattering option on this list.

Professor Preeti Arya, PhD, specializes in textile development at the Fashion Institute of Technology. She says that the right fabric for leggings depends on your needs. But if you're worried about maintenance, "you can go for something that is petroleum-based because care is easy," she says. Petroleum-based fabrics include spandex, polyester, and nylon. These options are also typically much cheaper, according to Arya, but you can also opt for wool or silk, which sometimes feel better on your skin since they're natural fibers. An attacker emptied the Ethereum vault of cross-chain DEX Chainflip, looting about $4.86 million in ETH and stablecoins and sending it to Tornado Cash, apparently by using a legitimate signing key.

Cross-chain decentralized exchange Chainflip Chainflip (FLIP) paused its protocol on Saturday morning after security firms detected an attack which looted about $4.86 million in ETH and stablecoins from its Ethereum-based vault, apparently using a valid signature from the protocol's own signing key.

"We're aware of a potential exploit affecting Chainflip vaults," the protocol shared on X. "As a precaution, the protocol is being put into full safe mode. Deposits, withdrawals, swaps and quoting are disabled."

Chainflip's FLIP token plummeted about 34% following the 2:10 a.m. ET exploit, per The Block's Chainflip price page. The token's market capitalization dropped from about $41.6 million to $27.1 million as of publication time.

Security firm Decurity first shared details of the attack on X through its Defimon Alerts bot. The alert noted Chainflip's Ethereum vault was drained of "its entire liquid balance," making up 520.2 ETH, 3.25M USDC and 758K USDT worth around $4.86 million at the time. The alert said that rather than exploiting a smart contract bug, the attacker apparently obtained access to the validator network's aggregate signing key, meaning the secret code that authorizes transfers.

The attacker launched the hack through a fresh wallet, and later sent nearly all the proceeds through mixing protocol Tornado Cash, per security firm AMLBot. "The laundering was executed with high-speed automation," AMLBot stated, noting that the stablecoins moved too fast for USDC issuer Circle and USDT issuer Tether to freeze the tokens, as the whole attack took place in under 10 minutes.

Chainflip has not said how the attacker may have compromised the key, which is jointly controlled by the protocol's 150 validators and rotated every three days; the last rotation happened on Nov. 18 at 4:53 p.m. ET, about two and a half days before the exploit. No one validator is supposed to have access to the full key; rather, each holds a piece and 100 out of 150 are required to sign transactions.

Blockchain data firm Bitquery noted in its investigation that Chainflip's key changed about an hour and 45 minutes after the theft. The timing suggests Chainflip rotated the compromised key to prevent further thefts, though Bitquery noted that no conclusions can be drawn from timing alone.

In another quirk Bitquery noted, the attacker's transaction carried a strange nonce, or a unique number that every Chainflip withdrawal is stamped with. That number, each of which is only used once, usually increments by one to prevent anyone from replaying old transactions, but rather than having a nonce around 315,000 like other transactions around that time, the attacker's nonce was a 39-digit number.

That suggests the approval wasn't made through Chainflip's normal system, which would have handed out the next number on the counter, but that the attacker somehow produced a valid signature outside that system. Bitquery noted that the drain was the only one of 299,677 signatures since 2023 that broke the count.

Chainflip's vaults on other chains like Bitcoin and Solana were apparently unaffected by the attack. However, a transaction on the Bitcoin network moved the nearly 10.5 BTC from a previous Chainflip vault address to a brand new address about two hours after Chainflip paused the protocol, suggesting another way the protocol is safeguarding its remaining funds, though its purpose has not been confirmed. That transaction has not yet been reported by security firms.

Chainflip previously suffered an exploit on Sept. 12 that saw an attacker abuse a flaw in how Chainflip processed Tron transaction memos to double-process six withdrawals on the Tron network.

The protocol's validators later voted to reimburse the affected liquidity providers (LPs) using the protocol's "surplus funds," which Chainflip described as "a combination of many things. It is both excess funds held by the protocol through gas fee interactions, assets sent to Chainflip in error that the protocol could not automatically return, and other sometimes so far unexplained surpluses that have built up in the vaults since launch."

Chainflip has not said whether it plans to reimburse the victims of the current hack. Chainflip did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Block.

#5074. Navigating the Unpredictable Ride of COPD

When COPD flare-ups affect breathing and health-related quality of life, ask about other treatment options.

HOOVES THUNDER AGAINST packed dirt as the bull bucks to the left and the rider leans right, tightening his grip on the rope. Just as he finds his balance, another sudden buck or turn can change the course of the ride.

The unexpected twists and turns of a bull ride may feel familiar to people living with inadequately controlled chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Not knowing when breathing challenges or a flare-up—a period when breathing becomes more difficult than usual that can last for several days—might occur can make everyday life feel unpredictable.

Mark H., 60, has experienced the challenges that can come with COPD since he was diagnosed in 2010. “COPD isn’t easy to navigate, and it can be a frightening condition to face,” he says. “I tried to ignore my diagnosis early on because I didn’t want to believe it, and I didn’t want to think about how it might affect my life. But ignoring it didn’t stop my COPD from making itself known. Shortness of breath was really impacting my day to day.”

With support and clinical intervention, Mark was able to better manage his COPD and get back to doing more of the things he loves. Now, he wants others living with COPD to know help is available to manage their condition.

COPD IS A complex and progressive disease that can make breathing more difficult over time.

COPD can be caused by inflammation in the airways that causes damage to parts of your lungs. Patients with COPD may also have chronic bronchitis and/or emphysema.

People with COPD can experience persistent cough, excessive mucus production, wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. Understanding COPD is important, and recognizing when the disease may not be adequately controlled is critical. Living with uncertainty around flare-ups can carry an emotional weight as well, says Corinne Young, nurse practitioner, pulmonary disease specialist, who is the Founder/Executive Director of the Association of Pulmonary Advanced Practice Providers.

Flare-ups, also known as exacerbations, are the worsening of COPD symptoms over several days. They can happen to anyone with COPD. During a flare-up, difficulty breathing, wheezing, and coughing can intensify and take longer to resolve. Even one flare-up can lead to permanent lung damage.

Young, who in addition to seeing patients, competes in team roping at rodeos, knows the importance of paying attention to changing conditions—a perspective she brings to helping patients recognize when their COPD may be inadequately controlled.

“The biggest predictor of a flare-up is a previous flare-up, and they start to get closer and closer together,” Young explains. For example, someone may experience a flare-up or exacerbation once every two years, then once a year, then every six months, then every three. “Inflammatory responses in the body drive these exacerbations, and that may lower lung function,” Young adds. That decline can increase the risk of additional flare-ups, perpetuating the cycle.

AS MARK’S COPD became more difficult to manage, it increasingly interfered with the life he was used to living. Shortness of breath and frequent flare-ups made it harder to work, travel, and do as many of the things he enjoyed. Eventually, he made the difficult decision to retire early from his job as a field service engineer.

Even after stepping away from work, Mark continued to struggle with his COPD. “I remember feeling like, ‘Well, I guess this is my life now,’” he says.

IN THE FALL of 2024, Mark underwent a pulmonary function test, bracing for bad news. The results confirmed that his current treatment plan was no longer adequately managing his COPD, prompting a discussion with his pulmonologist about what to do next. His doctor explained that Mark’s high eosinophil count could be a sign of type 2 inflammation. With this information, Mark and his doctor explored other treatment options, including Dupixent® (dupilumab).

Dupixent is a prescription medicine used with other medicines for the maintenance treatment of adults with inadequately controlled COPD and a high number of blood eosinophils (a type of white blood cell that may contribute to your COPD). Dupixent is used to reduce the number of flare-ups and can improve your breathing.

Dupixent is not used to relieve sudden breathing problems and will not replace an inhaled rescue medicine.

Do not use if you are allergic to dupilumab or to any of the ingredients in Dupixent.

Dupixent can cause serious side effects, such as allergic reactions, including skin reactions, that can sometimes be severe, eye problems, and joint aches and pain.

Please see additional Important Safety Information below.

Mark noticed a difference after adding Dupixent. “I could breathe better,” he says. Now, Mark feels less winded, and he’s doing more of the things he loves. “I’m really grateful that I can enjoy my hobbies more without constantly thinking about my COPD,” he adds.

For Mark, better breathing started with an honest conversation. Young encourages anyone living with COPD to be open with their healthcare provider, who can explain the full range of treatment options available. “It’s not just inhalers anymore—there are a lot of options,” she says.

Like bull riders who stay alert to changing conditions, people living with COPD can watch for signs that their disease may be inadequately controlled and talk with their doctor about their treatment options. With the right support, they may be able to enjoy more of the moments that matter to them—including, for some, time spent in the rodeo stands.

IMPORTANT SAFETY INFORMATION & INDICATION

Dupixent is a prescription medicine used with other medicines for the maintenance treatment of adults with inadequately controlled COPD and a high number of blood eosinophils (a type of white blood cell that may contribute to your COPD). Dupixent is used to reduce the number of flare-ups and can improve your breathing.

Do not use if you are allergic to dupilumab or to any of the ingredients in DUPIXENT®.

Before using DUPIXENT, tell your healthcare provider about all your medical conditions, including if you:

Tell your healthcare provider about all the medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements.

Especially tell your healthcare provider if you are taking oral, topical, or inhaled corticosteroid medicines or have COPD and also have asthma. Do not change or stop your other medicines, including corticosteroid medicine or other asthma medicine, without talking to your healthcare provider. This may cause other symptoms that were controlled by those medicines to come back.

DUPIXENT can cause serious side effects, including:

The most common side effects in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease include injection site reactions, common cold symptoms (nasopharyngitis), high count of a certain white blood cell (eosinophilia), viral infection, back pain, inflammation inside the nose (rhinitis), diarrhea, stomach problems (gastritis), joint pain (arthralgia), toothache, headache, and urinary tract infection.

Tell your healthcare provider if you have any side effect that bothers you or that does not go away. These are not all the possible side effects of DUPIXENT. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You are encouraged to report negative side effects of prescription drugs to the FDA. Visit www.fda.gov/medwatch, or call 1-800-FDA-1088.

Use DUPIXENT exactly as prescribed by your healthcare provider. It’s an injection given under the skin (subcutaneous injection). Your healthcare provider will decide if you or your caregiver can inject DUPIXENT. Do not try to prepare and inject DUPIXENT until you or your caregiver have been trained by your healthcare provider.

Please see accompanying full Prescribing Information including Patient Information.

Learn more about Dupixent at Dupixent.com/COPD.

#5073. GameStop CEO Says Digital-Only Games Have ‘Hurt Consumers’ as GTA 6 Skips Discs

GameStop CEO Says Digital-Only Games Have ‘Hurt Consumers’ as GTA 6 Skips Discs

GameStop CEO Ryan Cohen has criticized video game publishers for abandoning physical discs, as Grand Theft Auto 6, one of the most anticipated games ever made, launches on Thursday as a digital download only.

"When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it or lend it to a friend," Cohen told Bloomberg. "Unquestionably, the decision to move to all digital has hurt consumers, and it's also hurt GameStop."

Cohen declined to name specific companies, but Take-Two Interactive is releasing the $80 game only as a download, with retailers selling boxes containing download codes. Asked about presales, Cohen said: "It's a code in a box. I mean, we're selling a lot of it."

Take-Two declined to comment to Bloomberg.

The shift hits a core part of GameStop's business. Pre-owned and refurbished products made up 22% of the retailer's sales, about $171 million, in the quarter that ended August 1, down 32% from a year earlier, according to Bloomberg.

Cohen said he has spoken with publishers, who he argued benefit from limiting trade-ins because used copies compete with new sales. "They're taking away competition," he said.

Sony announced in July that it will stop producing physical discs for new PlayStation games in January 2028, a move experts have said will hit low-income gamers hardest. PlayStation founder Ken Kutaragi has dismissed the backlash as a "mentality issue," while an Infinity Ward veteran said publishers have pushed to cut discs since 2007.

Cohen said he has met with Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-NY), who is backing the Power to the Players Act, which would require gaming companies to give consumers ongoing access to the titles they buy. "A game that can be taken away the moment a company pulls the plug is not a purchase. It is a rental disguised as a sale," Torres said in October.

In Europe, the Stop Killing Games campaign gathered 1.3 million signatures for a European Citizens' Initiative calling for publishers to keep games playable after support ends.

The question of whether buyers own digital games has also reached the courts. Sony has argued in court that digital games can't be owned, prompting some in the crypto industry to pitch blockchain-based ownership as a fix.

Cohen's GameStop has also made bets beyond gaming. The company bought 4,710 BTC for more than $500 million in 2025, and in March moved all but one of them into a covered call strategy on Coinbase Prime to generate income. In May, after eBay rejected its takeover offer, GameStop sought shareholder approval to raise its authorized share count to 2.5 billion as it built a stake in the online marketplace.

#5072. Cyber investigating suspected $1 million bridge exploit as Upbit, Bithumb freeze transfers

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Upbit and Bithumb froze CYBER deposits and withdrawals as tokens pulled from the Ethereum bridge for Binance Labs-backed firm Cyber, formerly CyberConnect, were sold for about $968,000 in ETH.

Cyber, the social-focused Layer 2 network formerly known as CyberConnect, said Saturday that it is investigating "unexpected minting" of its CYBER CyberConnect (CYBER) token on Solana, which was followed by a transfer of CYBER out of its bridge's Ethereum lockbox. South Korean exchanges Upbit and Bithumb suspended CYBER deposits and withdrawals shortly after noon ET, citing a suspected security incident.

In an X post at 1:25 p.m. ET, Cyber said its team is checking which assets and bridge routes are affected. It asked users to hold off on using the CYBER bridge or depositing CYBER to exchanges, and said they don't need to migrate tokens, connect wallets or sign anything.

Upbit's caution notice linked two transactions. In the first, 5,213,000 CYBER was minted on Solana at 11:13 a.m. ET. Two minutes later, the same amount left CyberTokenAdapter, the Ethereum contract that holds CYBER for the token's LayerZero bridge, and went to a wallet that had been funded for the first time less than an hour earlier.

That wallet and a second one sold most of the tokens for ETH over the next hour through KyberSwap and MetaMask Swaps, mostly in clips of 150,000 CYBER at a time. At 12:40 p.m. ET, they sent 575.29 ETH to a fresh address, where it was still sitting as of publication. Another roughly 412,000 CYBER went to three addresses that block explorers haven't labeled.

CYBER fell about 8% to $0.2024 as the tokens were sold, before recovering to about $0.213, according to The Block's Cyber price page as of publication time. Bithumb said CYBER trading would continue during the freeze, and Upbit issued a trading caution rather than halting trading.

Cyber started out as CyberConnect, a social graph protocol that raised a $10 million seed round co-led by Multicoin Capital and Sky9 Capital in 2021. The CYBER token launched through Binance Launchpool in August 2023, and Binance Labs, now known as YZi Labs, later made a follow-on investment in the project. In May 2024, CyberConnect rebranded as Cyber and launched an Ethereum Layer 2 network for social apps built on Optimism's OP Stack, spinning off its Link3 app as a separate brand.

Earlier this month, Cyber said it had bought back about $13 million worth of CYBER over the past year. The Block has reached out to Cyber for further comment.

#5071. The Man With No Butt

My flat ass has haunted me since high school. So I did what any man would do and sought out some wisdom from the Internet. This is the story of my midlife butt crisis.

I REMEMBER THE first time I became aware of it. Or should I say lack of it.

I grew up in the mid '80s. A magical time. MTV actually played music videos. New Coke was a thing people cared about. And a ginger-headed German teenager named Boris Becker—Boom-Boom, to his millions of fans—became, at age 17, the youngest player ever to win Wimbledon.

While other kids my age were collecting Garbage Pail Kids cards or trying to solve Rubik’s Cubes, I was rewatching VHS recordings of Becker’s matches. I practiced his signature serve motion in front of my bedroom mirror. I begged—actually begged—my parents for the complete Boris Becker starter kit: the Ellesse tennis outfit, the Puma half-top sneakers, and the holy grail itself: the Puma Super tennis racket.

The problem was, no matter how hard I tried, no matter how much Hi-C I consumed, I could never quite achieve the same explosive spring that made Boom-Boom so spectacular. Then I noticed something about Becker’s serve—the one that earned him his nickname. Most players bent their knees to generate power. Becker did something else.

He stuck out his butt. Like, really stuck it out. His serve motion involved this pronounced posterior thrust that helped him achieve that devastating topspin and pace.

I went to the bedroom mirror. Turned sideways. Attempted the same motion. And that’s when it hit me with all the force of one of Becker’s 130-mph serves: I didn’t have a butt to stick out. Where Becker had curvature, I had...continuity. My back just sort of continued into my legs.

Reality set in. No bum-bum, no boom-boom.

By high school, I had pivoted to more cerebral pursuits like creative writing and a burgeoning interest in art history. Art history seemed safe—just looking at old paintings and Roman sculptures, right? Wrong. It became immediately clear that every civilization in human history had one thing in common: great asses.

One fateful morning during my sophomore year, I was standing at my locker wearing a pair of saggy-bottomed Gap khakis when I heard giggles behind me. The distinctive sound of teenage girls discovering something hilarious and vaguely cruel.

“He has no butt!” another voice announced with the confidence of a scientist making a groundbreaking discovery. More giggling. Then came the death blow that would echo through the halls of my high school for the next two and a half years:

Sure, it wasn’t the most creative nickname, but it had just enough alliteration to spread like a pre-internet meme. From that day on, I knew “they” knew.

I RECENTLY TURNED 50. I’m happily married and have two amazing kids. Life is good, but I’d be lying if I said the ghost of No-Butt Bender doesn’t haunt me. As I’ve aged, what little I had has somehow continued to erode. My wife loves me despite my anatomical deficiency but remains perpetually baffled by the lack of rear topography. And what was once giggles from teenage girls is now full-throated hysterical laughter from my 13- and 11-year-old children when they catch a glimpse of me in anything form-fitting.

Recently, Instagram’s insecurity algorithm served me up an ad for Perk men’s clothing. Their website is a gallery of flattering middle-aged bum-shots, but what really stopped my scroll was the pitch for their pants: “Our chinos magically turn even a flat butt into a compliment magnet. Whether you’re 25 or 65, that never gets old!”

You have to understand—when you have no butt, no pants are flattering. So when Perk starts advertising pants that promise to be so bootylicious you’ll receive compliments everywhere you go, I dared to dream. I did what any man starved for posterior validation does—panic-ordered chinos in every damn color.

The moment the package arrived, I tore it open. I slipped them on, turned toward the mirror, and—holy hell—was that…something? An actual curve? A protrusion? I squinted. I turned. And I practically sprinted to the living room where the family was waiting and struck a pose.

Crickets. Then a full collapse into hysterical laughter.

“I’m sorry,” my wife gasped between laughs, “but those pants are working so hard and getting nowhere.”

I was tired of feeling like the only person other than Hank Hill to be cursed with diminished gluteal syndrome (DGS). It’s a very isolating condition. But I figured if Perk could build an entire company around flat-figured men, there had to be others out there, living their lives in quiet resignation.

Close to midnight on a Wednesday, my face lit only by the glow of my computer, I did the obvious: Googled “men with no butts.”

The search results led me to a Reddit post titled, “Gentlemen, how do you live with having no butt?” This guy laid it all out: approaching 29, finally accepting his glute-free reality, enduring constant jokes from his girlfriend, the whole nine yards of tush-less trauma. But what really got me was his closing line: “Please help.”

I stared at those two words. They contained decades of my own experience—the loneliness, the confusion, the desperation. This post was five years old, but I didn’t care. I had to reach out.

I woke the following morning to find his response waiting like a message from a long-lost brother: “You seem legit I guess. Sure why not.” We were already bonding!

I asked Ross (names have been changed to protect the in-ass-cent) what motivated him to publicly post about his crisis on Reddit, and he said, “It was a genuine problem and if someone’s got an answer that helps, I was going to be all ears.”

Ross first became aware of his DGS when a friend at the gym dropped the bomb: “Dude, you have no ass whatsoever.” The keen observation sent Ross into a spiral of photographic evidence review. He started examining pictures of himself and came to the only possible conclusion: “Huh, I guess I don’t.” It was his own bedroom-mirror moment.

As for the wisdom he received from the Reddit hivemind, he said it was mostly people prescribing the usual suspects: sprints and squats: “I was doing a shit ton of those back then and still do,” he told me. Five years later, he reports modest gains: “It’s no dump truck but I’ve got a little bit of cushion for comfort back there.” He eventually broke up with the ass-teaser (good riddance) and has been dating a new lady who actually pinches it every now and then—a gesture that, for men like us, feels like winning the Mega Millions.

But the struggle continues. Despite his Stairmaster devotion, sweatpants still “kind of sag” making it look like he may have taken a small dump in them. Still, Ross gave me the faintest glimmer that improvement was possible. Maybe a guy with no butt could transform it into a bona fide ba-donk-a-donk.

I phoned two lifelines from my past—Jonathan Botts, MD, a college friend who’d become an orthopedic surgeon at the Los Angeles Orthopedic Institute in Sherman Oaks, California, and Derek DeGrazio, Britney Spears’s former physical trainer, who had whipped me into the best shape of my life for my long-ago wedding and now is a partner at Barry’s Bootcamp Miami.

Dr. Botts (who inexplicably escaped high school without a single butt-related nickname) broke down the anatomy: the butt consists of three muscles—the gluteus maximus, medius, and minimus—but it’s the maximus that does the heavy lifting in filling out a man’s pants.

When I asked about the possibility of maximizing my non-existus, he didn’t sugarcoat it. “Here’s the problem: You can’t go from what you are now to just working on your butt and developing a huge butt,” he told me. “People are doing lots of protein intake and protein shakes and bulking up like that. You could get bigger and your butt would get bigger with you. Muscularly. But I don’t know. I don’t think you could take huge leaps with just doing squats and lunges.”

So basically, I’d need to become the Hulk to grow a butt.

Derek offered an alternate strategy with what he calls the Bender Big Three™. “I can’t say for certain, but I think No-Butt Bender can become Mild-Butt Bender with squats for foundation, Romanian deadlifts to pop your glute a little bit, and a nice hip thrust,” he said.

Mild-Butt Bender. It did have a certain je ne sais quoi.

Derek, who freely admits he was born with “a great Italian ass,” is my gluteal bizarro from an alternate universe where only perfect butts exist. He told me his seat meat gave him confidence in high school, something I could only imagine by taping Springsteen’s Born in the USA album cover to the back of my pants. Derek played baseball, a sport notorious for its revealing tight pants. “I don’t know if they came to watch baseball or if they came to watch us in our uniforms,” he recalled, misty-eyed.

I hated him. I loved him. I wanted to be him.

But then—plot twist!—just as I began fantasizing about playing shortstop, Derek dropped a bomb: “I started to realize that what was a blessing at one point became also my Achilles heel at the same time. If there is a downside, I wasn’t the fastest guy on the team.”

Wait. There was a downside to having a butt?

Dr. Botts, who describes his own posterior as “bigger than average,” delivered the final revelation: Having a bigger butt doesn’t automatically mean you have a stronger butt. “If you have a small butt, does that mean you have weak glutes? It doesn’t at all. You can have a big butt and have really weak glutes.”

All these years, I’d associated my small butt with weakness. With inadequacy. With being less than. What if I was wrong? What if, beneath my perpetually drooping pants lurked a superhero-strength posterior more powerful than even Derek’s celebrated Italian ass?

Unlikely. And who am I kidding? It’s not like if I had said to those girls in high school, “Oh no, you don’t understand—it’s really strong!” they would have stopped laughing and made out with me.

But hey, this new knowledge gives me something to cling on to. Wish I could say the same for my pants. Still, I am what I am. I am No-Butt Bender. And if that makes my kids laugh and my wife give me a warm, “It’s okay. I love you anyway” hug, I’ll take it.
